standard: ASME B1.1 Unified Inch Screw Threads (UNC/UNF series); tap drills per the published machinist tables named in sources
sources: PREMSA Industries, "Tap & Drill Size Chart - UNC, UNF, Metric Tap Drills", https://premsaindustries.com/en/resources/tap-drill-size-chart (read 2026-08-13)
RivCut, "Tap Drill Chart: Inch + Metric Sizes (UNC/UNF/ISO)", https://www.rivcut.com/resources/tap-drill-chart (read 2026-08-13)
notes: The pitch column here is THREADS PER INCH, an integer count, not a length. hole_standards reports it as `tpi` and also as `pitch` in millimetres (25.4 / tpi) so a caller that only speaks pitch is not silently handed a count.
coarse_pitch names the FIRST-CHOICE series for the size, which for Unified inch threads is UNC. It is the tpi, not a millimetre pitch.

The tap drill is a SHOP number, not a standard: it is the stock drill nearest ~75% thread engagement, and the drill DESIGNATION (#7, F, 27/64) is part of the callout an operator reads, not a rounding of a decimal. Only rows where both sources print the same drill and the same decimal ship.

Casualties of the two-source rule, recorded so nobody thinks they were forgotten: #0-80 UNF (no #0 UNC exists, so the size would have a fine thread sitting in the first-choice slot), #5-44 UNF, #12-28 UNF, 11/16 and 15/16 UNC, 11/16-24, 13/16-20, 7/8-14 and 15/16-16 UNF, and everything above 1 in. Each appears in one source only.
tap_drill is the diameter to BORE for a cosmetic/tapped hole. It is NOT the radius to bore when fusing real thread geometry - see the CHEATSHEET rule about boring at root_radius for real threads.
